summary.headline: India's defence electronics market is valued at roughly USD 10.5 billion (2025) and growing near 8% CAGR -- the fastest of any major country -- while the broader India battery market stands at about USD 9.3-14 billion and is set to more than quadruple to USD 78.8 billion by 2035 on EV, grid-storage and telecom demand.
key_takeaways: India's defence production hit a record ₹1.27 lakh crore in FY24 (up 174% since FY15) and defence exports surged 34x since FY14 to ₹23,622 crore in FY25, with government targets of ₹3 lakh crore production and ₹50,000 crore exports by FY29.

BEL dominates India's defence electronics with a 60% market share and INR 730 billion order backlog (Q3FY26); HAL, BDL, MDL and a fast-growing cluster of private players (Data Patterns, Astra Microwave, Apollo Micro Systems, Paras Defence) round out the ecosystem.

India remains the world's largest/second-largest arms importer even as domestic defence electronics content rises toward 74%+ for leaders like BEL, reflecting both import substitution progress and continued reliance on foreign engines, GaN/semiconductors and critical minerals.

The India battery market is overwhelmingly import-dependent for lithium, cobalt and nickel (India imports ~84% of lithium-ion batteries from China/Hong Kong), even as PLI-backed gigafactories (Tata, Reliance, Exide, Ola) target 50+ GWh of domestic cell capacity.

Global defence spending (~USD 2.7 trillion in 2024, +9.4% real) and India's own 6.4% CAGR budget growth (2024-30E) are the key tailwinds, while engine/semiconductor supply delays (e.g., GE F-404 for Tejas) and China's near-total control of battery material supply chains are the key risks.
summary.report_markdown:
## Market size and trajectory
India's defence electronics market is estimated at **USD 10.48 billion in 2025**, forecast to grow at the **highest country-level CAGR (~8.0%) in the world** through 2035 (GM Insights), while other estimates put it at USD 7.46-7.5 billion (FY25) rising to USD 11.35-12 billion by FY32. India's overall defence sector produced a record **₹1.27 lakh crore in FY24** (up 174% since FY15) and is targeted to reach **₹3 lakh crore by FY29**. Defence exports hit an all-time high of **₹23,622 crore in FY25**, a 34x jump since FY14. Separately, India's battery market -- spanning lead-acid, lithium-ion, EV, grid storage and defence/telecom applications -- is sized at roughly **USD 9.3-14 billion (2025/26)** and projected to reach **USD 78.81 billion by 2035** (22.6% CAGR), driven by EV adoption, renewable storage and telecom backup needs.

## Segments
- **By process/architecture (defence electronics):** C4ISR systems command ~40% share globally and are the largest equipment segment; radar & multi-function sensors led with 31.6% share in 2025; electronic warfare is the fastest-growing sub-segment (~7-8.7% CAGR).
- **By platform:** Airborne dominates (39-47% of global defence electronics revenue); land, naval and space follow, with space the fastest-growing platform (~7.2-7.3% CAGR).
- **By application (India defence electronics):** Navigation/communication/display led India's market in 2024; electronic warfare was ~22.6% share.
- **By battery technology (India battery market):** Lead-acid retained 53.2% share in 2025 even as lithium-ion secondary batteries lead growth (65.5% revenue share, 15.9% CAGR); automotive is the largest application (39.6% share).
- **By defence production ownership:** DPSUs/public sector contribute ~74-79% of India's defence production value; private sector contributes 21-22%, but private firms punch above their weight in exports (68-98% of India's defence exports historically have come from private players, though recent PIB data shows DPSU exports catching up at 42.85% growth in FY25).

## Growth drivers
- **Government self-reliance push:** Positive Indigenisation Lists (5 lists covering 5,000+ items, 3,000+ already indigenised), 75% of modernisation capital earmarked for domestic procurement, FDI liberalised to 74% automatic / 100% government route.
- **Rising defence budgets:** India's defence budget rose from ₹2.53 lakh crore (FY14) to ₹6.81 lakh crore (FY26, +9.5% YoY); India's defence expenditure is projected to grow at 6.4% CAGR 2024-30E versus 4.2% in 2017-24, outpacing the global 5% CAGR.
- **Export ambition:** Government targets ₹50,000 crore in defence exports by FY29/2030, backed by BrahMos deals (Philippines), Akash exports cleared to 9 countries, and growing private-sector export share. - **EV and renewable storage buildout:** PLI-ACC scheme (₹18,100 crore outlay, 50 GWh target), PM E-DRIVE scheme (₹10,900 crore), and gigafactory investments from Tata, Reliance, Ola Electric and Exide are catalysing India's lithium-ion ecosystem.
- **Platform modernisation programs:** QRSAM, Project Kusha, P-75(I) submarines, AMCA fighter, LCA Tejas Mk1A/Mk2 and naval shipbuilding provide multi-year order visibility for BEL, HAL, BDL, MDL and private electronics suppliers.

## Tailwinds
- Global defence spending reached USD 2,718 billion in 2024 (+9.4% real, steepest rise since Cold War), with NATO's 2025 Hague commitment targeting 5% of GDP by 2035 -- lifting global export demand for Indian platforms like BrahMos.
- India's 75% domestic-procurement mandate and 509+ import-banned items create captive demand for domestic defence electronics and battery suppliers.
- Falling lithium-ion pack prices (global pack prices to USD 80/kWh by 2026) improve EV and grid-storage economics even as India imports most cell inputs.
- Operation Sindoor (2025) validated indigenous Akash and S-400 systems in live combat, reinforcing confidence in Indian-made air-defence electronics.

## Headwinds
- **Import dependence on critical inputs:** India imports ~82% of lithium and ~76% of silicon from China; battery-grade graphite, cobalt and nickel remain almost fully import-dependent, exposing manufacturers to Chinese supply-chain leverage (China controls 85-98% of global capacity across cathodes, anodes, separators and electrolytes).
- **Engine and semiconductor delays:** GE F-404 engine delivery delays for Tejas Mk1A and broader semiconductor shortages have pushed back key platform deliveries by months.
- **India remains the world's largest/second-largest arms importer** despite indigenisation gains -- a structural dependence that will take years to fully unwind.
- **China's battery oversupply and price undercutting** compress margins for domestic Indian cell manufacturers, who face 25-40% higher near-term costs than Chinese imports.
- **US ITAR and export-control regimes** limit depth of technology transfer even under dual-sourcing arrangements like the India-US TRUST initiative.
- **Procurement delays:** complex acquisition procedures add 3-5 years to typical capital-equipment procurement cycles in India.

## Value chain
- **R&D/design:** DRDO (50+ labs) and private players (Data Patterns, Astra Microwave) lead product design; BEL invests 6-7% of revenue in R&D annually.
- **Component/sub-system manufacturing:** BEL, HAL, BDL and Tier-2 private suppliers (Apollo Micro Systems, Paras Defence) produce radars, EW suites, missiles and sub-systems; semiconductor and GaN inputs remain import-reliant.
- **System integration:** BEL and HAL serve as lead integrators for large platforms (QRSAM, Tejas), capturing higher margins than pure component suppliers.
- **Battery value chain:** Cathode/anode/electrolyte materials are overwhelmingly imported (China ~39-60% share of key materials); India assembles cells and packs domestically with PLI incentives but lacks upstream mining/refining scale.
- **Export/offset:** Defence offset policy requires 30% reinvestment in India for large foreign contracts, pushing OEMs like Thales, Safran and Rafael into Indian JVs.

## Players
Key listed/major players include **Bharat Electronics (BEL)** -- market leader in defence electronics with 60% share and ₹730 billion backlog; **Hindustan Aeronautics (HAL)** -- India's sole fighter-platform integrator; **Bharat Dynamics (BDL)** -- missile systems leader; **Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders (MDL)** -- premier naval shipyard; and fast-growing private players **Data Patterns, Astra Microwave Products, Apollo Micro Systems, Paras Defence & Space Technologies**. In batteries, **Exide Industries, Amara Raja Energy & Mobility, Tata (Agratas), Reliance New Energy, Ola Electric and HBL Power Systems** lead domestic manufacturing, while global giants LG, Panasonic and CATL hold technology and scale advantages.

sections.heading: Executive summary
prose: India's defence electronics market is worth roughly USD 10.5 billion in 2025 and is growing near 8% a year, the fastest rate among major countries. Alongside it, India's broader battery market, currently USD 9.3-14 billion, is expected to more than quadruple to USD 78.8 billion by 2035, driven by electric vehicles, grid storage and telecom demand.

Indian defence production hit a record Rs 1.27 lakh crore in FY24, up 174% since FY15, and defence exports have surged 34 times since FY14 to Rs 23,622 crore in FY25. The government is targeting Rs 3 lakh crore in production and Rs 50,000 crore in exports by FY29.

State-run Bharat Electronics (BEL) dominates defence electronics with a 60% market share and a Rs 730 billion order backlog, supported by HAL, BDL, MDL and a fast-growing group of private players. India is still one of the world's largest arms importers, and the battery sector remains heavily dependent on imported lithium, cobalt and nickel, mostly from China -- the central tension in both industries' growth stories.

sections.heading: Market size & growth
prose: India's defence exports reached an all-time high of Rs 23,622 crore in FY 2024-25, a 34-fold increase from Rs 686 crore in FY 2013-14. Growth has been steady and sharp across the decade: from Rs 4,682 crore in FY17 to Rs 10,746 crore in FY19, Rs 15,918 crore in FY23, Rs 21,083 crore in FY24, and now Rs 23,622 crore in FY25.

Defence exports grew at roughly 28% CAGR between FY18 and FY24. The India defence electronics market itself is forecast to grow at about 7-8% CAGR through FY32, among the fastest rates of any major country's defence electronics sector.
The government has set a target of Rs 3 lakh crore in total defence production and Rs 50,000 crore in exports by FY29, implying continued strong growth from current levels.

sections.heading: Segments
prose: Globally, C4ISR systems are the largest defence electronics equipment segment, exceeding 40% share in 2025. Radar systems make up 23.3% of the global defence electronics market, while electronic warfare is the second-largest and fastest-growing application segment, at about 22.6% of India's defence electronics market in 2024.

By platform, airborne systems lead globally with 39.4% share, while land platforms account for roughly USD 58.9 billion and are growing at about 4.9% CAGR. In India's defence production base, public-sector DPSUs contribute around 74-79% of output, with the private sector contributing 21%.

In batteries, secondary (rechargeable) batteries lead India's market with 65.5% revenue share in 2025 and a 15.9% CAGR outlook through 2031. Lead-acid remains the dominant chemistry at 53.2% share, while automotive is the largest end-use application at 39.6% share, growing at 15.2% CAGR through 2031.

sections.heading: Value chain
prose: Design and R&D sit with DRDO's 50+ labs and private firms like Data Patterns and Astra Microwave, which design radars, electronic warfare systems and missile electronics. BEL invests 6-7% of revenue in R&D each year. Domestic, R&D-heavy production carries 40-45% gross margins, far above the 8-10% margin typical of build-to-print export orders.

Component and sub-system manufacturing runs through BEL, HAL, BDL and Tier-2 private firms such as Apollo Micro Systems and Paras Defence, though critical semiconductor and GaN content remains import-reliant. Defence electronics makes up roughly 32% of total global defence procurement value.

BEL and HAL act as lead system integrators on major platforms like QRSAM, Tejas and Project Kusha, managing complex multi-vendor projects at a scale private players cannot yet match -- a role that supports BEL's roughly 27-28% EBITDA margins.

In batteries, cathode, anode and electrolyte materials are overwhelmingly imported, with China alone supplying 39% of global cathode material by weight. India assembles cells and packs domestically under PLI incentives but lacks upstream mining and refining scale, keeping domestic cell costs 25-40% higher than imports.

Defence offset policy requires foreign OEMs to invest 30% of large contract value (Rs 2,000 crore or more) back into India, pushing global firms like Thales, Safran, Rafael and MBDA into joint ventures with Indian players.

sections.heading: Key players & positioning
prose: Bharat Electronics (BEL) is the clear leader in Indian defence electronics with a 60% market share and a Rs 730 billion order backlog as of Q3FY26. Hindustan Aeronautics (HAL) is India's sole fighter-platform integrator, supporting nearly 80% of the country's active military fleet, with an order backlog of roughly Rs 1.8-2.4 trillion. Bharat Dynamics (BDL) is the primary manufacturer of guided missiles, with access to over 50% of the domestic missile market, while Mazagon Dock (MDL) is India's leading shipbuilding yard and the only PSU shipyard to have built both destroyers and submarines.

A fast-growing cluster of private players is emerging alongside the PSUs. Data Patterns commands the highest margins among peers through a modular, reusable component approach with over 1,000 COTS building blocks. Astra Microwave is a proxy play on India's defence and space growth via its RF/microwave sub-systems and Rafael joint venture. Apollo Micro Systems has worked with DRDO for over 40 years across missile and naval programs, and Paras Defence is the only Asia-Pacific company making submarine periscopes and the only Indian private firm producing hyperspectral cameras. Larger private conglomerates -- Tata Advanced Systems, Mahindra Defence and L&T Defence -- are also expanding across electronics, aerostructures and missile systems.
Globally, Lockheed Martin (12.8% share) and RTX Corporation (13.3% share) lead the worldwide defence electronics market in 2025, with no significant India-specific share disclosed for either.

In batteries, Exide Industries leads nationally and has commissioned a 3 GWh lithium-ion line in Pune, while Amara Raja dominates southern India and supplies batteries for defence communication and surveillance uses. Tata (via Agratas/Tata Chemicals) is investing about USD 1.5 billion in a lithium-ion gigafactory in Gujarat. HBL Power Systems supplies specialised lead-acid, nickel-cadmium and lithium-ion batteries for defence and railways, and Attero Recycling is India's largest lithium battery recycler, expanding capacity toward 200,000-300,000 tonnes a year.

sections.heading: Margins
prose: BEL's EBITDA margin has expanded steadily from 21.2% in FY20 to 28.8% in FY25, and management guides to about 27% EBITDA margin from FY26 onward. This reflects BEL's position as a lead system integrator managing complex, large-scale projects.

Domestic defence orders generally carry 40-45% gross margins, compared with just 8-10% for export or build-to-print orders, as seen at Astra Microwave. Among private players, Data Patterns shows the highest margins -- 38-45% EBITDA -- thanks to its modular, reusable COTS-based approach.

sections.heading: Supply & capacity
prose: India's PLI-backed Advanced Chemistry Cell (ACC) scheme targets 50 GWh of domestic lithium-ion cell manufacturing capacity, with gigafactories being built by Tata, Reliance, Exide and Ola. Despite this build-out, India remains overwhelmingly import-dependent for lithium-ion batteries: imports of lithium-ion batteries rose sharply from USD 329 million in 2017 to USD 1,193 million in 2020, and USD 1,291 million in just the April-December period of FY22.
To support domestic manufacturing, India raised the import duty on lithium cells from 5% to 10% and on lithium battery packs from 5% to 15%, both effective April 2021.

sections.heading: Tailwinds vs headwinds
prose: Global defence spending rose 9.4% in real terms in 2024 to USD 2,718 billion, the steepest annual increase since the Cold War, lifting demand for Indian platforms and exports. Domestically, a 75% procurement mandate for domestic suppliers and 509 import-prohibited defence items create captive demand. Falling global lithium-ion pack prices -- toward USD 80/kWh by 2026 from USD 115/kWh in 2024 -- improve EV and storage economics even as India scales domestic cell manufacturing. Operation Sindoor in May 2025, which neutralized 600 hostile drones using indigenous S-400 and Akash systems, validated Indian systems in live combat and boosted both domestic and export confidence.

Despite indigenisation progress, India remains the world's second-largest defence importer, accounting for roughly 9% of global arms imports during 2020-24. On the battery side, India imports about 82% of lithium and 76% of silicon from China, which controls 85-98% of global capacity across cathodes, anodes, separators and electrolytes -- a major structural vulnerability. Domestically manufactured battery cells are expected to cost 25-40% more than Chinese imports in the near term due to oversupply and price undercutting from China.

Engine and semiconductor supply delays -- notably GE F-404 engine deliveries for the Tejas Mk1A -- threaten platform production timelines and underline continued dependence on foreign licensed technology. Complex, multi-stage acquisition procedures add 3-5 years to typical procurement cycles, delaying order conversion into revenue, while US ITAR export-control regimes limit the depth of technology transfer available to Indian firms even under dual-sourcing arrangements.

sections.heading: Outlook
prose: India's defence electronics market is set to keep growing near 8% a year through FY32, supported by rising defence budgets (6.4% CAGR projected for 2024-30E, up from 4.2% in 2017-24), a 75% domestic procurement mandate, and long-term platform programs like QRSAM, Project Kusha, AMCA and Tejas Mk1A/Mk2 that give suppliers multi-year revenue visibility. Government targets of Rs 3 lakh crore in production and Rs 50,000 crore in exports by FY29 signal continued expansion of both domestic output and global sales.

The battery market's growth to USD 78.8 billion by 2035 depends on EV adoption, grid storage and telecom demand, backed by PLI-funded gigafactories targeting 50+ GWh of cell capacity. However, this growth will likely continue alongside heavy import dependence on Chinese lithium, cobalt, nickel and processed materials, keeping near-term domestic cell costs 25-40% above imports.

Key risks to watch: continued reliance on foreign engines and semiconductors (illustrated by GE F-404 delays), China's near-total control of battery material supply chains, slow multi-year procurement cycles, and ITAR-related technology transfer limits. These will shape how quickly India's indigenisation targets convert into실현 production and export outcomes.

prose: This report draws on Indian government data (PIB), industry research firms (Mordor Intelligence, GM Insights, 6Wresearch, Market Research Future, MarknTel Advisors), sector analysis from HDFC Securities, and supporting technical and policy documents from NITI Aayog, DCX India and Nishith Desai Associates.

source.snippet: Global military expenditure rose 9.4% to USD 2,718 billion in 2024, the steepest annual increase since the end of the Cold War

tailwinds.point: 75% domestic-procurement mandate and 509+ import-banned defence items create captive demand for Indian suppliers.

source.label: Mordor Intelligence
source.snippet: 509 import-prohibited items anchor captive demand for Indian suppliers

tailwinds.point: Falling global lithium-ion pack prices (toward USD 80/kWh by 2026) improve EV and storage economics even as domestic cell manufacturing scales up.

source.label: Mordor Intelligence
source.snippet: Global pack prices fell to USD 115 per kWh in 2024 and are trending toward USD 80 per kWh by 2026

tailwinds.point: Operation Sindoor (2025) validated indigenous Akash and S-400 air-defence electronics in live combat, boosting confidence in Indian systems both domestically and for export.

source.label: Mordor Intelligence
source.snippet: Operation Sindoor in May 2025 neutralized 600 hostile drones, validating indigenous S-400 and Akash systems under live combat conditions

headwinds.point: India remains the world's largest/second-largest arms importer despite indigenisation progress, with India accounting for ~8.3-9.8% of global arms imports (2019-24).

source.label: HDFC Securities
source.snippet: the world's second-largest defence importer (~9% share of global imports during 2020–24)

headwinds.point: India imports ~82% of lithium and ~76% of silicon from China, with China controlling 85-98% of global capacity across cathodes, anodes, separators and electrolytes -- a major structural risk for the battery value chain.

source.label: Mordor Intelligence / IndianDefenseNews
source.snippet: China’s dominance is overwhelming. It controls between 85% and 98% of global capacity

headwinds.point: Engine and semiconductor supply delays (e.g., GE F-404 for Tejas Mk1A) due to geopolitical friction threaten platform production timelines and highlight continued dependence on foreign licensed technology.

source.label: HDFC Securities
source.snippet: continued delays in GE F-404 engine deliveries due to geopolitical friction pose a significant threat to production timelines of Tejas MK1A

headwinds.point: China's battery oversupply and price undercutting mean Indian locally manufactured battery cells are expected to cost 25-40% more than imports in the near term.

source.label: IndianDefenseNews
source.snippet: Locally manufactured cells are expected to cost 25–40% more than imports in the near term

headwinds.point: Complex, multi-stage acquisition procedures add 3-5 years to typical India defence procurement cycles, delaying order conversion into revenue.

source.label: Mordor Intelligence
source.snippet: Complex acquisition procedures add 3-5 years to average procurement cycles

headwinds.point: US ITAR export-control regimes limit the depth of technology transfer available to Indian defence electronics firms even under dual-sourcing arrangements.
